resources.string: Auntie Fai cooks over charcoal in ski goggles, and has done for decades. The queue is long and the omelette is expensive, but no other street stall in the world holds a Michelin star.
Frying pad thai over charcoal since 1966, and still drawing a queue down Maha Chai Road every night. Order it wrapped in a thin egg blanket, with orange juice on the side.
A civil-servant canteen favourite that grew into a city institution. The stir-fried crab with yellow chilli is the dish people come back for.
Thai drinking food tucked behind Wat Pho, in a courtyard hung with old enamel signs. Everything is grilled, fermented or pickled, and built to be shared.
Chef Thitid Tassanakajohn cooks in memory of his grandmother, on a rooftop above the Old Town. Book weeks ahead, and take the tasting menu.
A restored shophouse on the river with Wat Arun lit up across the water. Come for the view, stay for the crab curry.
A Yaowarat fixture serving peppery kuay jab in a clear, punishing broth. The rolled rice noodles are the whole point.
Chinatown comfort food since 1959. Braised goose over rice, dim sum steamers, and noodles served long past midnight.
Green-shirted staff, plastic stools, and prawns grilling on the pavement at Soi Texas. Loud, cheap, and exactly what Yaowarat is for.
Chef Pam cooks Thai-Chinese memory inside her family\'s 120-year-old shophouse, once a Chinese pharmacy. The menu is built around five elements.
Named for the ratio of Thai ingredients to everything else. A small kitchen doing serious things with produce most restaurants overlook.
A curry bar on Charoen Krung run by three friends who met in fine-dining kitchens. Order the southern curries and expect real heat.
Roasting duck in the same Bang Rak shophouse since 1909. Order it over rice, with a bowl of broth on the side.
Modern Thai in a converted shophouse off Silom, and once ranked the best restaurant in Asia. The river prawn is the dish to order.
Southern Thai cooking taken as seriously as anywhere in the world, with ingredients driven up from Trang and Phuket. The hardest table in Bangkok to book.
Twin brothers cooking modern German food in a 1970s house with a garden. Not what you expect in Bangkok, and better for it.
Isaan cooking from Ubon Ratchathani, pounded to order in a mortar you can hear from the street. Start with som tum pu pla ra if you can take it.
French technique on the river at Icon Siam, with Wat Arun framed in the window. The most formal meal on this list, and dress accordingly.
The pink-shirted khao man gai stand near Pratunam market. Poached chicken, rice cooked in the fat, and a ginger-chilli sauce doing the heavy lifting.
Queue numbers are handed out before opening for a reason. The mama tom yum arrives as a mountain of pork, seafood and instant noodles.
Thai fried chicken buried under a drift of crisp fried garlic, a short walk from Lumphini Park. Order sticky rice and som tum alongside.
Progressive Indian food served as a wordless emoji menu, with the chef conducting the room. Theatre and cooking in equal measure.
Bee Satongun rebuilds recipes from old Thai cookbooks using modern technique. Precise, balanced, and unlike anything else on this list.
A Sukhumvit noodle stall so popular it split into two shops side by side. Order it dry, with everything in it.
The beef broth in the vat out front has been topped up and simmered for decades, never once emptied. Order the beef noodle soup and taste what that does.
Trat and Isaan Thai · Thong Lo
Home cooking from Trat and Isaan, built on the owner\'s grandmother\'s recipes. The moo chamuang, pork stewed with sour chamuang leaves, is the one.
Roman cooking in a Sukhumvit side street, with a porchetta that would hold its own in Testaccio. Sunday lunch is the move.
Proper Neapolitan pizza from a wood-fired oven, certified by the Naples association. The margherita is the test, and it passes.
A tiny Ekkamai counter with a long waiting list and fish flown in from Toyosu. Omakase only, and worth planning a month around.
A family home turned restaurant, cooking close to zero-waste with produce from its own garden. A quiet, generous way to finish the month.
